lesson_title: The Crow, the Ramp and the Quarter Turn
hook_text: Why does flipping a fraction and switching its sign make a perfect right angle? Watch the quarter turn.
clip_script: Here's a rule you've probably used without knowing why: to get a perpendicular gradient, flip the fraction and switch the sign. Four thirds becomes minus three quarters. Feels like a spell, right? It's actually a quarter turn, and you can watch it happen. A gradient of four thirds is a little staircase triangle: three blocks across, four blocks up. Now grab that triangle and rotate it ninety degrees. The across becomes the up. The up becomes the across. Your new staircase: four across, three up — the fraction flipped itself. And the climb changed direction — what went uphill now comes downhill — so the sign switches. Flip and switch is just a rotation, written in numbers. Multiply the two gradients: four thirds times minus three quarters. The fours cancel, the threes cancel, and you're left with minus one. Every perpendicular pair does this — every single one. That's the corner test: two sides of a triangle, multiply their gradients, and if minus one appears, you've proved a right angle without ever touching a protractor. One little rotation, and thirty marks of analytical geometry start making sense.
visual_style: A staircase triangle on grid paper — three across, four up — physically rotating a quarter turn with a satisfying snap; numbers cancelling in a multiplication until only minus one remains, stamped like a seal.
mood: Curious and satisfying, a trick revealed as machinery.
pacing: Hook the spell first, slow through the rotation so it lands, quick triumphant finish on the cancelling.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and own every gradient rule instead of memorising it.
